idiom_name: zero-size struct types (struct{} / named empty type) + embedding
implementation_notes: Go's baseline layout already gives the pattern's goal: an empty struct type has width 0 (unsafe.Sizeof(struct{}{}) == 0), a struct composed only of zero-size fields is zero-sized as well, and the runtime short-circuits zero-byte allocations to a shared zerobase. Stateless behaviour is carried by a named empty type with methods and promoted into the host by embedding it, so the methods join the host's method set while adding no storage; the classic empty base is replaced by this zero-size embeddable type. Type-level, not instance-level, configuration belongs in the type itself or in a package-level value - never in a struct field.
pitfalls: A zero-size field as the last field of a struct is padded with an extra word (struct{ x int64; z struct{} } is 16 bytes), so placement decides whether the saving survives.
All zero-size values may share one address and the spec permits it, so pointer identity or pointer arithmetic on them is meaningless - never use it as a tag.
Embedding is not inheritance: promoted methods cannot see the host's state, and embedding two types with a same-named method makes the selector ambiguous.
